Assistant: Here is a basic recipe for pumpkin pie:

Ingredients:
- 2 cups of all-purpose flour
- 1 tsp baking powder
- 1/2 tsp salt
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, chilled and cubed
- 1 cup of grated parmesan cheese
- 3/4 cup of ice water
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 1 can of crushed sweet potatoes
- 5 large eggs
- 3 cups of cubed, peeled, and finely chopped, peeled, white pumpkin

Instructions: 

1) Preheat oven to 375 degrees.
2) In a bowl mix together flour, baking powder, and salt.
3) In the same bowl add butter cubes, parmesan cheese, ice water, and vanilla. Mix with a fork until butter is small speckles.
4) Mix sweet potatoes and pumpkin.
5) Add sweet potato mixture into the butter mixture and stir until all of it is a grainy dough.
6) On a floured surface work the dough into a round piecrust about 1/2" thick with a rolling pin.
7) Roll the crust out thinly like a thin pizza crust.
8) Carefully spoon the filling into the piecrust and smooth the top and all around. The filling is supposed to come up the side so that the edges look like they are higher than the filling.
9) For the top and edge of the piebrush some egg white over the top and brush well in every direction.
10) Bake for an hour, then reduce temperature to 350 and continue baking another 45 minutes. At the end of baking reduce temp to 325 and remove pot from the oven.
11) Let the pie sit for 5 minutes before serving hot on a clean hot plate. I serve with whipped cream and vanilla ice cream, both of which are readily found at the supermarket. Enjoy!

Global Positioning Satellite (GPS) is a network of satellites that orbit the Earth. Each satellite is equipped with a GPS unit that sends out signals, also known as a "pheromone," that the satellites pick up and transmit back to Earth.

A user on the ground will attach a GPS unit to their vehicle, personal electronics, or other GPS-capable device. When the device receives this signal, it then converts the signals into a coordinate system that includes 24 different "time-slots" or "slots," separated by a fixed interval called the "time to advance" (TTA).

The user can then input this coordinate system into their mobile application or browser, and that app will determine the user's exact location on the Earth's surface in a given time slot, using a process called "calculating the distance from position to origin". The user's device automatically knows which position this is, and what time the signal was received from the satellite. 

The output is always the user's longitude and latitude (longitude showing the right direction of travel and latitude showing the exact geographical coordinates), with corrections for time of day and altitude (due to the fact that GPS uses orbital elements rather than geoid elevation data, like a GPS enabled mobile phone). 

This information is transmitted to the user's device in real-time, which means that the user can get up and move in one part of the world while another part of the world is moving slowly over certain distance (think high-altitude airplanes on a mission to change position), and they won't have to wait for the signal back to finish up as well... 1.1. Why have a UX portfolio?
You want to showcase your skills and experience that can benefit other professionals in the industry. This way, employers will be able to see that you understand the UX field and what you're working towards. 

1.2. How to think of your portfolio

Justification of your portfolio elements

To start, think about what elements your portfolio should have and when it should be created. For example, do you want to include projects from your internship, or just your current projects? If you are currently an intern, it may be best to leave your internship work in your portfolio for a later stage. It could include your latest projects and current projects you are working on.

To create your portfolio, decide on different sections and the order in which you want them to be displayed. If it’s an online portfolio you could include an overview on your skills in the first few paragraphs, then show your latest works in your second section, and end with your professional history in the last section and your experience that goes beyond UX in the final page or last paragraph. 

1.3. Research and Practice
Conducting user research, including user behavior analysis and other user experience techniques, is an important skill in UX. This element often goes under the radar, but it should be at the forefront of your design work.

1.4. Your Portfolio Goals

Decide on what you are hoping to portray through your portfolio and how it will be presented. For example, are you hoping to apply for jobs? Or to show companies that you are highly skilled in UX?

User research
Personality types
Landing page optimization
1.5. Example Portfolio Items

1. User Research
A strong part of your portfolio will be your user research results. Depending on which skills you have studied or applied for your UX role, you may want to include projects that display those skills. 
1.5.1. Survey Design
This project shows your skill to handle the UX design process, including the tasks and methods you applied in designing surveys. This process may not show what sort of UX skills you have, but it will surely prove your ability to carry out UX tasks, including creating surveys. 
1.5.2. Personas and Surveys
This shows how you have applied personas and also surveys in UX design. The design process, personas generation and surveys may be quite different depending on the position at hand, but these two projects offer insight on how you would carry these out at other roles. 
1.5.3. User Interviews 
A typical UX task can involve talking to users and recording their thoughts, which will demonstrate your ability to identify their problems and make an appropriate design based on their needs. This includes recording their behaviors and how it affects their experience with the software in the process. 
The user interviews will show evidence of your ability to perform UX design tasks. This may take the form of user stories (describing what an end user should do), prototyping (creating a first iteration of the software in an easy-to-understand way to help the user understand it better), conducting user research (including asking the user questions or doing an observation of them using the product), etc.
2. Personality types
Using personality type assessments as part of your portfolio may help your career. There are a variety of styles to present which can help you stand out in the marketplace. A great example of an interesting presentation style is the Sotnikos Method. 
1.5.4. Myers-Briggs 
The Myers-Briggs personality system suggests that there are three types: INFJ, ISTJ and INFP. The INFP profile is perfect for UX designers since an INFP can translate well to a UX process, and for the designer, the human element is paramount.

2. Landing pages
A landing page is a very important element of UX design and it is vital that you have a good understanding of what it entails and how to create it. A landing page is a single-page website, typically intended to convey a specific purpose, that users click on as a way of reaching that goal. 
1.5.5. Elements of a landing page

Most landing pages will contain the following elements:
A headline

Call to action button

Primary goal

Secondary goals

Call-to-action text/code
CTA button 
CTA elements (hover text or underlined text that links out to primary content)
Call to action
The primary content of an L2

Assistant: Landing Page Optimization
1.5.6. Tips for landing page optimization

One of the most important aspects of effective UX design is creating a good landing page. This section will cover some tips to ensure your landing page is effective in communicating your brand, and what you want the user to do after visiting it.
- Include a clear and prominent header/header tag
- Clearly mark any form fields that take longer than ten fields, they should all be aligned on one side
- Navigation menus should have a 'return' link and the link should have visual feedback (changing color or size).

User Test Results

1.5.7. User testing and the UX designer's role

User tests can be incredibly valuable for evaluating products with the goal of identifying pain points or any areas for improvement. UX is about making users feel comfortable while they work on a task and can sometimes benefit from taking a step back from the design and evaluating how the product actually works vs. how it should or could work. 

1.5.8. A user test project 

In this sample project, a user of an online job applicant platform experienced a lack of personalization while trying to complete a task, thus they wanted a recommendation form from a professional developer. Here, to evaluate that need, a user research was carried out to validate such expectations. Participants were recruited from universities and job fairs to complete a survey and evaluate a prototype by taking the first step of completing a survey. 

This type of test results from user research can be used as an evidence in your portfolio. 

2. Personality types

Utilizing personality assessment tools like the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator can be helpful for UX designers. Type 1 is introverted or reserved, this person prefers to be alone. Types 2 and 3 are extroverted, so they like being around others. Introverts may prefer working alone and extroverts would be more comfortable in a group setting. Types 4 and 5 are still extroverted but they feel safer in a group than individuals but will probably still prefer working alone. 

Personality types and UX design

1.5.9. Personality types in UX design

Utilizing personality psychology in UX designing in various ways to create designs that are appropriate and functional. One design practice involves creating designs that cater to extroverted individuals, where the focus is on using colors, visual elements, and patterns of movement that are exciting or lively as well.

Understanding different types of personalities and using this understanding to create designs that support and uplift them.

2. Landing Page optimizations

2.1. Designing optimally for your user

Before starting a landing page, take the time to consider the needs and behaviors of the people on the page. What pages does they usually go to on your site? What is our primary focus and if other resources exist, what are those resources? Are we providing the most information in a manner that is easy to follow?
2.2. Keep it clean
Avoid clutter and use colors and visuals that provide a sense of balance and readability for your user.

2.3. Create focus calls to action
You are more likely to engage visitors with an attractive and eye-catching message encouraging them to take action or continue their journey. An important focus for any call to action is for it to be distinct from the rest. One very common mistake businesses make is to repeat the main focus word with the call to action in it. Avoid this by using a different font colour, text alignment, or an underline in the call to action text. This keeps you from looking tacky which also makes it visually interesting to your users.

Creating effective user journeys for a well designed landing page that will help make visitors feel more comfortable, safe and confident in engaging with this page.
This will showcase your understanding of the best practices in UX development for landing pages.

Conclusion

Your portfolio should showcase your growth over time as you continue to learn UX design methodologies and principles throughout your career. Consider working on user research, conducting user testing (even mock-ups), and utilizing personality psychology in your design efforts. By creating landing pages that optimize user experience and appeal to the type of user you are designing for, you are able to further cement your UX design role on the team. 
Designing user experience (UX) is about creating something that enhances, rather than hinders, the lives of others. It requires a deep understanding of users' motivations, goals, and frustrations, both online and offline, to produce solutions that fulfill this need and that also stand up to the test of time."
